strengths: The paper studies a clean and relevant gap in online fair division: approximate PROP1 when stronger notions such as EF1 and MMS are known to be hard online. The focus on maximum item value predictions is a natural and relatively lightweight information model.

The manuscript contains several conceptually useful results: negative examples for natural greedy rules, a randomized guarantee against non-adaptive adversaries, and an algorithmic result under perfect/noisy MIV predictions. The structure makes clear how these settings relate to adaptive versus non-adaptive adversaries.

The paper is mostly self-contained, with definitions, adversary models, related work, and appendix proofs included. For a theory paper, reproducibility is mainly proof reproducibility, and the authors provide enough detail to follow many of the arguments.
weaknesses: Several proof and notation issues materially weaken confidence in the technical claims. For Theorem 9, the constant/algebra around alpha appears inconsistent: the proof needs alpha proportional to 1/log(n/delta), but the displayed derivation includes expressions that read as exp(-27 alpha / 128) while equating this to exp(-log(n/delta)). The claim that alpha <= 1/4 for all n >= 2, delta in (0,1) is also false for the stated constant if alpha = 27/(128 log(n/delta)). These may be fixable, but they affect a central theorem.

Theorem 11 and Algorithm 1 suffer from presentation and consistency problems. The potential function is written with different denominators in the prose and algorithm/proof, and the proof includes apparent sign/name errors for phi-plus and phi-minus. Because this theorem is the main positive result, these issues make the central contribution difficult to verify reliably.

Some impossibility proofs appear to rely on adaptive construction details that are not always stated cleanly. Proposition 10 defines future valuations using the evolving allocation, but the adversary model and whether such dependence is allowed under the prediction assumptions should be made explicit. There are also apparent case-label typos such as Case 2 using |A1| > 0 when it should distinguish |A1| > 1.

The significance is moderate rather than high for ICML. The paper is purely theoretical and does not connect strongly to learning methodology beyond the learning-augmented framing. The MIV prediction model is interesting, but the achieved 1/n-PROP1 guarantee is weak, and the paper leaves the main advice-free approximation question open.

The limitations discussion is brief and mostly in the conclusion. It honestly identifies the main open problem, but the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of when MIV predictions are realistic, how one-sided overestimation might be obtained, and whether the adaptive adversary model is appropriate for the motivating applications.

Presentation needs polishing: there are many spacing/grammar issues, inconsistent notation, and multiple places where proof sketches in the main text obscure key assumptions. No ethical concerns are apparent, but the paper also does not include an explicit ethics or broader impact discussion.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful gap in online fair division: approximate PROP1 is a natural weaker benchmark after known impossibility results for EF1 and MMS, and the distinction between adaptive/non-adaptive adversaries is well motivated.

The main directions are conceptually sensible: negative examples for natural greedy rules, a high-probability guarantee for uniform random allocation against a non-adaptive adversary, and an algorithm using maximum-item-value predictions.

The manuscript includes appendices with full proof attempts for most stated results, and the algorithm is specified explicitly enough that the theoretical contribution is at least partly reproducible.
weaknesses: The technical presentation contains many serious proof and notation problems that undermine confidence in soundness. For example, the proof of Theorem 9 has algebraic mistakes in Lemma 15's bounded-difference argument; the proof of Theorem 11 contains inconsistent definitions of phi-plus/phi-minus and an apparent erroneous claim that phi_i^+ = phi_i^- = phi_i^{k+1}-1; and Proposition 10 has case-condition errors such as treating |A_1| > 0 as a second case after already assuming g_1 is allocated to agent 1. Some may be fixable typos, but their density makes the central claims hard to verify reliably.

The inapproximability proof for stronger notions appears especially fragile. It uses valuations depending on the algorithm's allocation history, but the adversarial model for that proposition is not stated precisely enough, and parts of the PROPX derivation seem algebraically invalid or at least incorrectly written. Since these results are used to position PROP1 as the meaningful boundary, this is a material weakness.

The learning-augmented framing is oversold. The paper explicitly lacks robustness in the usual advice-free sense, handles only one-sided overestimation error, and assumes access to future maximum item values without a convincing model for obtaining these predictions. This weakens the significance of the MIV result relative to the stated motivation.

The contribution is specialized and largely theoretical, with no empirical or simulation evidence to show whether the randomized allocation or MIV-based algorithm has useful behavior beyond worst-case bounds. This is not fatal for a theory paper, but it limits the practical significance for an ICML audience.

The writing is not acceptance-ready. There are frequent grammatical errors, spacing issues, inconsistent notation, repeated proof sketches instead of clean theorem statements in the body, and multiple equations whose extracted or rendered form is confusing. These issues materially affect verifiability rather than being merely cosmetic.

Limitations and ethics are treated only superficially. The conclusion mentions an open question, but there is little discussion of the realism of prediction assumptions, deployment risks in fair allocation systems, or the consequences of using approximate fairness guarantees in high-stakes settings.

strengths: The paper studies a well-motivated gap in online fair division: approximate PROP1 when stronger notions such as EF1 and MMS are known to be impossible. The problem formulation is clear and the focus on weaker maximum-item-value predictions is a meaningful refinement over prior normalization-information assumptions.

The contributions form a coherent picture: impossibility for natural greedy strategies under adaptive adversaries, a randomized guarantee against non-adaptive adversaries, and a deterministic MIV-prediction algorithm against adaptive adversaries. This gives useful structural insight into what information or adversarial restrictions make online PROP1 approximation possible.

The MIV-prediction result is technically interesting. The potential-function algorithm is nontrivial, uses only lightweight side information, and the extension to one-sided prediction error is a valuable learning-augmented-style robustness statement.

The manuscript is generally readable, with helpful motivation, related-work positioning, and an honest conclusion noting that advice-free PROP1 approximation remains open. I do not see material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Several proof and notation issues should be fixed before others can confidently build on the results. In Theorem 9, the constant-level Bernstein calculation appears to contain typographical or algebraic inconsistencies around whether alpha is 27/(128 log(n/delta)) and the exponent should involve 1/alpha; the claim that alpha <= 1/4 for all n >= 2 also appears false without adjusting constants or taking a minimum.

The proof of Proposition 10 in the appendix appears to have more serious gaps or typos. The case split says Case 1 |A1|=1 and Case 2 |A1|>0, which overlaps and likely should be |A1|>1. The subcases seem to miss or inconsistently handle t=n+1. Some final inequalities in Case 2(b), especially the exponent manipulation involving K and alpha, are not convincing as written and may be incorrect.

The main algorithm section has avoidable inconsistencies: the text says p=(p1,...,pm) when it should be over agents, the displayed potential before Algorithm 1 differs from the algorithm/proof in the n^2+n+1 term, and the proof sketch reverses or confuses the meanings of phi-plus and phi-minus relative to the appendix. These are probably fixable but currently reduce confidence.

The achieved deterministic guarantee is only 1/n-PROP1, i.e. a value threshold of vi(G)/n^2, and the paper does not provide tightness or lower bounds showing this dependence is necessary under MIV predictions. This limits the significance of the positive result.

The random-allocation theorem only holds against non-adaptive adversaries, while the strongest adversarial model remains largely unresolved. This is acknowledged, but it means the contribution is more of a useful step than a complete resolution.

As a theory paper, reproducibility mainly means proof checkability. The paper includes appendices, but because several arguments contain apparent algebraic and notation errors, the current version needs polishing and perhaps correction to be fully reproducible.
